title: THE CHURCH CALLED YOU TO SERVE JESUS… SO WHY DID YOU END UP FEELING USED?
paragraphs: THE CHURCH CALLED YOU TO SERVE JESUS… SO WHY DID YOU END UP FEELING USED?

When sacred service becomes unpaid labor, exhausted volunteers begin disappearing quietly—and the Church must confront a painful question: Are we making disciples of Jesus Christ, or simply finding people to keep our ministries running?
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.

It happens when you have spent years giving your time, sacrificing your weekends, missing family gatherings, spending your own money, and showing up for church responsibilities even when your personal life is falling apart.
You keep smiling.
You keep saying, “Yes, Pastor.”
You keep telling everyone, “It's all for the Lord.”
But somewhere between another late-night ministry meeting and another Sunday when nobody even asked how you were doing, something inside you began to break.
And the worst part?
You feel guilty for being tired.
Because how do you tell people you are exhausted from serving God without sounding like you no longer love Him?
How do you explain that you still love Jesus, still believe in the Church, still want people to be saved…
But you are beginning to dread the very ministry that once made your heart come alive?
Maybe you are the worship team member who has not experienced a Sunday simply sitting in God's presence for months.
Maybe you are the children's ministry teacher who spends every service caring for other people's children while quietly wondering who is discipling your own.
Maybe you are the media volunteer who arrives before everyone else, leaves after everyone else, and only hears from leadership when something goes wrong.
Maybe you are the usher, cleaner, driver, administrator, sound technician, prayer worker, or ministry assistant whose absence is noticed faster than your suffering.
And maybe the sentence you are most afraid to say is this:
“I don't think they care about me anymore. I think they only care about what I can do for them.”
If those words hurt, stay with me.
Because what Jesus teaches about serving, leadership, and the value of His people may change how you see your ministry forever.
And if you are a pastor or ministry leader reading this, please don't leave.
This is not an attack against faithful shepherds.
It is an invitation to examine whether the people entrusted to our care are being loved as disciples or managed as resources.
Because a church can have a full ministry calendar and still have volunteers with empty hearts.
It can celebrate tremendous attendance while overlooking the quiet suffering of the people who made those gatherings possible.
It can preach the love of Christ from a beautifully decorated platform while failing to practice that same love toward the exhausted people who decorated it.
And Scripture gives us no permission to ignore that contradiction.
Consider a moment in the Gospel of Mark that we sometimes read too quickly.
Jesus had sent His apostles into ministry. They had preached, served, and carried out the work entrusted to them.
When they returned, they gathered around Him and reported what they had done and taught.
And what did Jesus say?
Did He immediately assign them another project?
Did He rebuke them for needing rest?
Did He remind them how many people still needed ministry?
No.
He said:
“Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while.” — Mark 6:31, KJV
The Gospel explains that so many people were coming and going that the apostles did not even have leisure to eat.
Read that again.
They were serving.
The needs were real.
The crowds were waiting.
Yet Jesus recognized their need for rest.
The Greek wording is striking:
ἀναπαύσασθε ὀλίγον — anapausasthe oligon
“Rest a little.”
The verb anapauō, from which anapausasthe comes, means to rest, refresh, or find relief.
Jesus was not dismissing the needs of the crowds. In the very next verses, He would respond compassionately to the multitude.
But He did not treat the exhaustion of His disciples as irrelevant.
He cared about the workers, not merely the work.
And that distinction matters more than many churches realize.
Because somewhere along the way, some Christian communities have confused faithfulness with unlimited availability.
They have confused sacrifice with the inability to say no.
They have confused commitment with constant attendance.
And sometimes, without realizing it, they have created environments where volunteers feel more valued for their productivity than for their spiritual growth.
But a disciple is not a machine.
A brother in Christ is not a staffing solution.
A sister in Christ is not a ministry department's permanent emergency backup.
These are people purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ.
They have families.
They have responsibilities.
They have private battles.
They have prayers nobody hears.
And sometimes the person operating the sound system is silently begging God to save his marriage.
Sometimes the woman teaching children about God's faithfulness is struggling to believe God has not forgotten her.
Sometimes the smiling greeter at the church entrance is battling depression, grief, or financial hardship.
Yet everyone assumes they are fine because they keep showing up.
Until one Sunday…
They don't.
And suddenly the messages begin.
“Where are you?”
“Why weren't you at your post?”
“Who will cover your schedule?”
“We really need committed people.”
But the question that should have been asked long before they disappeared was much simpler.
“How is your soul?”
That is the question ministry leadership cannot afford to forget.
Jesus never taught that greatness in His Kingdom meant acquiring the most people to serve our ambitions.
He taught the opposite.
In Mark 10, James and John approached Jesus seeking positions of honor.
The other disciples became indignant.
Jesus gathered them together and confronted the world's understanding of authority.
He explained that worldly rulers often exercise power over those beneath them.
Then He declared:
“But so shall it not be among you.” — Mark 10:43, KJV
In the Greek text, the contrast is unmistakable:
οὐχ οὕτως δέ ἐστιν ἐν ὑμῖν — ouch houtōs de estin en hymin
“But it is not so among you.”
Jesus was establishing a radically different pattern for His followers.
Leadership in His Kingdom was not supposed to imitate the domination and status-seeking of worldly power.
He continued:
“But whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister.” — Mark 10:43, KJV
The Greek word translated “minister” is διάκονος — diakonos, meaning a servant or one who ministers to others.
And then Jesus gave the ultimate reason:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45, KJV
This is where the Gospel exposes every leadership model built on self-importance.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, did not enter this world demanding that everyone organize themselves around His personal comfort.
He came to serve.
He came to give.
He came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And His service was not a publicity strategy.
It led Him all the way to the cross.
Think about that.
The One who deserved all worship willingly took the position of a servant.
And yet some who claim to represent Him can become offended when volunteers ask for a weekend with their families.
Something is deeply wrong when ministry leaders expect sacrifices from others that they would never willingly make themselves.
Something is wrong when a volunteer's legitimate need for rest is automatically labeled rebellion.
Something is wrong when people are praised publicly for their faithfulness but privately pressured through guilt, fear, or spiritual intimidation.
And something is wrong when “Do it for Jesus” becomes a convenient way to avoid treating people with dignity.
Those words should never be used to silence someone who is being mistreated.
Because Jesus is not honored by using His name to justify behavior that contradicts His character.
Now, we need to be careful here.
The Bible absolutely calls Christians to serve.
It calls us to sacrifice.
It calls us to bear one another's burdens, to use our gifts for the good of the body, and to remain faithful even when ministry becomes difficult.
Galatians 5:13 tells believers to serve one another through love.
First Peter 4:10 teaches that we should minister our gifts to one another as stewards of God's grace.
And Galatians 6:9 encourages us not to grow weary in doing good.
Christian service is not supposed to revolve around personal convenience.
Sometimes love really does cost us something.
Sometimes faithfulness requires staying when leaving would be easier.
Sometimes we must serve without applause, appreciation, or immediate reward.
But none of those truths gives a leader permission to exploit another believer.
There is a difference between choosing sacrifice out of love and being pressured into sacrifice through fear.
There is a difference between carrying your cross and being forced to carry responsibilities that someone else refuses to share.
There is a difference between serving Christ faithfully and believing your worth to the Church depends on how much work you can perform.
Jesus calls His disciples to self-denial.
He does not command church leaders to deny the humanity of the people they lead.
And Scripture is remarkably direct about the spirit in which Christian leadership must operate.
Peter wrote to the elders:

“Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.” — 1 Peter 5:2–3, KJV
Notice that phrase.
“God's heritage.”
The people do not belong to the pastor.
They do not belong to the ministry director.
They do not belong to the institution.
They belong to God.
And the Greek expression behind the warning against domineering leadership is particularly revealing:
μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων — mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes tōn klērōn
“Not as domineering over those entrusted to you.”
The verb katakyrieuō carries the sense of exercising mastery or domination.
Peter is not forbidding leadership, accountability, correction, or appropriate authority.
He is forbidding the kind of leadership that treats God's people as possessions to control.
A shepherd does not own the sheep.
A shepherd is accountable to the Chief Shepherd.
And one day, every Christian leader will answer to the Lord Jesus Christ for how the people under their care were treated.
Not merely for how many programs succeeded.
Not merely for how impressive the attendance figures looked.
Not merely for how much money was raised.
But for whether they shepherded the flock faithfully.
Hebrews 13:17 reminds believers that leaders watch over souls as those who must give an account.
Souls.
Not merely schedules.
Not merely departments.
Not merely performance reports.
Souls.
There is another scene in Scripture that makes this even more personal.
In John 13, Jesus knew that His hour had come.
The cross was approaching.
His betrayal was near.
And during the meal, He rose, laid aside His outer garments, took a towel, and began washing His disciples' feet.
The Master knelt before His followers.
The Lord of glory performed a task associated with humble service.
Then He said:
“For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.” — John 13:15, KJV
Imagine how different some churches would become if leaders genuinely lived that verse.
What if the pastor occasionally helped clean the building alongside the volunteers?
What if ministry directors learned the names of volunteers' children and asked about their families?
What if leadership meetings included honest conversations about whether ministry schedules were sustainable?
What if people were encouraged to attend Bible studies, receive pastoral care, and grow spiritually rather than being perpetually assigned to another duty?
What if volunteers were allowed to say, “I need help,” without being made to feel spiritually inferior?
What if a struggling member could step away from a ministry role temporarily and still know they were loved, welcomed, and valued?
That would not weaken the Church.
It could help the Church become healthier.
Because people who are genuinely discipled are not merely more effective servants.
They are being formed into the likeness of Jesus Christ.
And that is the purpose.
Not simply filling positions.
Making disciples.
Jesus commanded His followers in Matthew 28:19–20 to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to observe His commands.
He did not commission His Church merely to create religious events that require an endless supply of exhausted volunteers.
The mission is to proclaim the Gospel and nurture people into faithful obedience to Christ.
Ministries are meant to serve that mission.
People are not meant to be consumed by the machinery of ministry.
And this is where some of us need to examine our own hearts as well.
Because not every exhausted volunteer has been exploited.
Sometimes we say yes when we should prayerfully say no.
Sometimes we want to be needed so badly that we take on responsibilities God never assigned us.
Sometimes we fear disappointing people more than we fear neglecting our own spiritual health.
Sometimes we quietly resent responsibilities we voluntarily accepted but never communicated that we could no longer sustain.
And sometimes we have confused being indispensable to a ministry with being faithful to Christ.
That is a dangerous confusion.
Because you were never meant to be anyone's savior.
There is already a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
And the Church does not stand because you never miss a Sunday.
It stands because Jesus Christ is its Head.
Colossians 1:18 declares that Christ is the Head of the body, the Church.
He is the One who holds His people together.
He is the One who builds His Church.
He is the One who saves.
You can be faithful without being constantly available.
You can love your church while establishing wise boundaries.
You can honor your leaders while respectfully communicating concerns.
You can serve sacrificially without pretending you have unlimited strength.
And you can acknowledge genuine mistreatment without abandoning your faith in Jesus Christ.
But please hear this, especially if you are wounded.
Do not allow the failures of imperfect Christians to become your final definition of Christ.
People may have misrepresented Him.
Leaders may have disappointed you.
A ministry may have taken more than it should have.
But Jesus is not the sum of the failures of those who claim His name.
He is the sinless Savior who died for sinners, rose again, and calls His people to repentance, reconciliation, and new life.
And if you have been deeply hurt, healing does not require pretending the harm never happened.
Forgiveness does not mean declaring sinful behavior acceptable.
Reconciliation may require truth, repentance, accountability, and restored trust.
Sometimes wise boundaries are necessary.
Sometimes a conversation with responsible church leadership can lead to meaningful change.
And when abuse, threats, or serious misconduct are involved, seeking appropriate outside help and protection is not a betrayal of Christ.
The Gospel does not ask us to protect appearances at the expense of truth.
It calls us to walk in the light.
First John 1:7 speaks of walking in the light as God is in the light.
And Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Both matter.
Truth without love can become cruelty.
But love without truth can become an excuse for allowing harm to continue.
The Church needs both.
There is a beautiful lesson in Acts 6 that we cannot overlook.
As the number of disciples increased, a complaint arose because certain widows were being neglected in the daily distribution.
This was not a minor inconvenience.
Real people were being overlooked.
And the apostles did not simply tell everyone to stop complaining and work harder.
They addressed the problem by establishing an appropriate distribution of responsibility, appointing qualified men to oversee the need.
The passage shows the importance of recognizing practical ministry problems and responding with wise organization.
Not every problem is solved by another sermon about commitment.
Sometimes the schedule needs to change.
Sometimes more people need to be trained.
Sometimes responsibilities need to be shared.
Sometimes a ministry needs to become smaller until it can operate without continually exhausting the same few people.
And sometimes a leader needs to say something that is surprisingly difficult:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Those words can become the beginning of restoration.
Because repentance is not only for people sitting in the congregation.
It is also for those standing behind the pulpit.
It is for ministry directors.
It is for volunteers.
It is for every believer who has allowed pride, resentment, control, selfish ambition, or fear to distort the way we love one another.
The cross leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
We all come to Jesus in need of mercy.
And the same grace that forgives us also teaches us to change.
Titus 2:11–12 describes God's grace as bringing salvation and instructing believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not permission to continue harmful patterns.
Grace calls us into transformation.
Now imagine a church where volunteers are not simply recruited but discipled.
Where a young man joins the media ministry and someone cares enough to teach him how to study the Bible, pray, and grow in character.
Where a single mother serving in children's ministry receives practical support rather than constant pressure.
Where an elderly usher is celebrated not merely for decades of attendance but for his testimony of faithfulness to Christ.
Where young volunteers are trained, encouraged, corrected lovingly, and given room to mature.
Where leaders notice when people are struggling before their ministry performance begins to decline.
Where serving is a joyful expression of belonging to Christ rather than a desperate attempt to prove one's worth.
And where rest is not interpreted as spiritual laziness.
Wouldn't that be a beautiful testimony to the world?
Not a perfect church.
There is no perfect congregation on this side of eternity.
But a repentant church.
A humble church.
A church where leaders and members alike are willing to be corrected by Scripture.
A church that remembers the people in the pews, on the platforms, behind the cameras, in the classrooms, and outside directing traffic are not disposable workers.
They are brothers and sisters for whom Christ died.
Paul wrote:
“And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.” — 1 Corinthians 12:26, KJV
The Church is a body.
Not a factory.
And when one part of the body is hurting, the answer is not to demand that it keep functioning until it collapses.
The answer is to care.
To listen.
To pray.
To support.
To restore.
To share burdens.
To remember that we belong to one another in Christ.
Galatians 6:2 says:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”
One another.
Those words matter.
Burden-bearing is not supposed to flow permanently in only one direction.
The volunteer who serves others also needs care.
The leader who carries responsibility also needs encouragement and accountability.
The pastor who ministers to the wounded also needs fellow believers who will pray for him and speak truth to him.
We need each other.
And above all, we need Jesus.
Perhaps you have been reading this with tears in your eyes because nobody knew how close you were to giving up.
You have not told anyone how much it hurts to feel invisible.
You have wondered whether your years of service mattered.
You have questioned whether God noticed the sacrifices nobody else remembered.
Let me remind you of Hebrews 6:10:
“For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister.” — KJV
God sees the labor of love done in His name.
Not every unnoticed act of service was wasted.
Not every difficult season was meaningless.
But this promise is not a command to remain indefinitely in a harmful situation.
It is a reminder that the Lord is just and faithful, even when human recognition is absent.
Your value was never created by your ministry position.
Your salvation was never earned by your volunteer hours.
And your place in Christ is not secured by how many responsibilities you can carry.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Notice the order.
Grace comes first.
Good works follow.
We do not serve to purchase God's acceptance.
We serve because of the grace He has given us.
That is the Gospel.

And if your ministry has quietly become an attempt to earn love, prove your worth, or escape the fear of disappointing others, perhaps Jesus is inviting you to remember where your identity truly begins.
Not in your title.
Not in your schedule.
Not in your achievements.
In Him.
There is a passage in Matthew 11 that feels especially tender here.
Jesus says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
In Greek, the invitation begins:
Δεῦτε πρός με — Deute pros me
“Come to me.”
And His promise includes:
κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς — kagō anapausō hymas
“And I will give you rest.”
In context, Jesus is calling the burdened to Himself and inviting them to take His yoke and learn from Him.
This is not a promise that discipleship will never involve suffering or demanding work.
It is an invitation into life under the gentle and humble Lord, whose way is fundamentally different from oppressive religious burden-bearing.
He does not invite us to become spiritually independent.
He invites us to come to Him.
And maybe that is exactly what you need today.
Not another assignment.
Not another demand.
Not another lecture about commitment.
But a renewed encounter with the Savior you began serving in the first place.
The One who knows your name.
The One who sees your tears.
The One who knows the motives of every heart, including yours.
The One who can expose what needs repentance, heal what has been wounded, and give wisdom for what must change.
And to the pastors and ministry leaders reading this, consider one question before your next volunteer meeting.
If every volunteer in your church stopped performing their assigned tasks for one Sunday, would you still know how to love them as members of Christ's body?
Would you know their struggles?
Would you know their spiritual needs?
Would you know whether they were growing in their relationship with Jesus?
Would they still feel welcomed and valued if they had nothing left to contribute?
These are not questions designed to humiliate leaders.
They are questions worth bringing before the Lord.
Because the greatest achievement of a church is not producing a flawless weekly program.
It is faithfully proclaiming Christ and nurturing people who know Him, love Him, and follow Him.
And to every volunteer who feels weary, I want to encourage you to do something courageous.
Speak honestly.
Not with bitterness.
Not with a desire to destroy.
But with truth and humility.
Ask for help where help is needed.
Seek wise counsel.
Make room for prayer, Scripture, family responsibilities, and genuine rest.
Examine your own motives.
Forgive where forgiveness is needed.
Pursue appropriate accountability where wrong has occurred.
And do not let your exhaustion convince you that Jesus has abandoned you.
If you have been serving out of fear rather than love, bring that fear to Him.
If you have become resentful, confess it to Him.
If you have used your authority to pressure or control others, repent before Him and seek to make things right.
If you have been wounded, ask Him for wisdom, courage, and healing.
Because this is where our story must always return.
Not merely to better volunteer management.
Not merely to healthier church systems.
Not merely to stronger leadership practices.
But to Jesus Christ.
Crucified for our sins.
Risen from the dead.
The Good Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.
The Lord who washes feet.
The Savior who restores sinners.
The Head of the Church who calls every one of us to follow Him.
This is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Even the story of a church volunteer who has forgotten what it feels like to be loved.
Even the story of a leader who must face the painful truth that good intentions do not excuse harmful actions.
Even the story of a congregation learning to replace pressure with discipleship, pride with humility, and appearances with genuine Christian love.
Jesus can rewrite those stories.
Not by pretending the damage never happened.
But through truth, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and transformed lives.
And if this article has exposed something in your own heart, please don't rush past that conviction.
Bring it to the Lord.
You do not need to disclose painful details to prove that your struggle is real.
Someone who is close to walking away may need to hear how the Lord helped you find wisdom, healing, and renewed faith.
Not to embarrass a church.
Not to attack a pastor.
But because there may be someone among your friends who has been silently asking whether anybody sees what they are going through.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow along.
Because our desire is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you draw closer to Him, I want to invite you into something more personal.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life of loving obedience, including generosity freely offered according to your ability and conviction.
But one meaningful way you can help glorify God is by supporting the faithful sharing of His Word.
We never want financial pressure to become another burden placed on the people of God.
The very message you have just read should remind us why that matters.
Support should flow from love, conviction, and willingness.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not manipulation.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
And discipleship should never be reduced to a transaction.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build a brand that people admire.
It is to point people toward the Savior who alone can redeem them.
Before you leave, I want to return to the person who started reading this article with a heavy heart.
The volunteer who is exhausted.
The pastor who is convicted.
The leader who knows something must change.
The believer who has been silently carrying resentment.
The person who loves the Church but has been deeply hurt by what happened inside it.
You are not beyond the reach of God's grace.
You can repent where you have sinned.
You can seek help where you have been harmed.
You can begin difficult conversations.
You can pursue restoration without denying the truth.
And you can return to Jesus, not because you have finally done enough for Him, but because He is the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
The Church belongs to Him.
The ministry belongs to Him.
Your life belongs to Him.
And His invitation still stands.
“Come unto me.”
So come.
Bring the exhaustion.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the questions.
Bring the guilt.
Bring the bitterness you need to surrender.
Bring the wounds you cannot heal by yourself.
Come to the One whose hands still bear the marks of His love.
And remember this:
Jesus did not shed His blood to turn you into disposable labor for His Church. He shed His blood to redeem you, make you His own, and teach you how to love and serve as someone who belongs to Him.
Never let the people who only noticed your empty ministry position make you forget the Savior who sees your entire soul.
